conceptTag: Netflix bets on its first original series
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Netflix, House of Cards 2011~2013) + 가상 적용 (회사 내 팀, 치킨 레스토랑)
insight: 대담한 베팅도 계산된 베팅일 수 있다. 업계 평균 확률에서 출발하되, 내가 가진 증거로 확률을 고쳐 읽고, 실패해도 버틸 수 있는 크기로 건다.
misconception: 큰 베팅을 한 회사는 결과를 확신했거나 무모했다. 실제로는 업계 평균 확률을 자기 상황에 맞게 고쳐 읽었을 뿐, 성공이 보장된 것은 아니었다.

sources.text: David Carr, "Giving Viewers What They Want," The New York Times, Feb. 24, 2013 (시청 데이터 활용, 파일럿 없이 2시즌 주문)
Netflix press announcement on House of Cards, March 2011, and contemporary trade coverage (Variety, The Hollywood Reporter) on the bidding and two-season order
Television Academy, 65th Primetime Emmy Awards (2013) nominations and winners
Media coverage, Oct.–Nov. 2017, of Netflix cutting ties with the show's lead actor

factChecks.note: 2011년 3월 Netflix가 파일럿 없이 2시즌 26편을 주문했다는 내용은 당시 보도와 NYT(2013) 기사로 확인하세요. HBO 등 다른 방송사가 관심을 보였다는 내용은 '보도에 따르면(reportedly)'으로 적었습니다.
2시즌 제작비 '약 1억 달러'는 널리 보도된 추정치이며 Netflix의 공식 수치가 아닙니다. 카드에 'reportedly around $100 million'으로 적었습니다.
House of Cards는 흔히 Netflix의 첫 대형 오리지널로 불리지만 Lilyhammer(2012년 2월)가 먼저 공개되었습니다. 그래서 카드에는 'one of its first original series'로 적었습니다.
전체 에피소드 동시 공개일 2013년 2월 1일, 2013년 에미상 주요 부문 후보 지명(스트리밍 전용 작품 최초)과 David Fincher의 드라마 감독상 수상은 Television Academy 기록으로 확인하세요.
NYT 기사에 나온 시청 데이터 논리(원작 BBC 드라마, Fincher 영화, 주연 배우 영화를 본 구독자 집단의 겹침)는 기사 표현 그대로 요약했습니다. 구체적인 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
2017년 주연 배우 관련 의혹으로 Netflix가 관계를 끊은 사실은 당시 보도로 확인하세요. 배우 이름은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Netflix skipped the pilot
body: In 2011, Netflix mostly streamed shows made by other studios. Then it promised to pay for two full seasons of a political drama, *House of Cards*, before a single scene was filmed.
TV networks usually test a show with one pilot episode first. Netflix skipped that step. It looked like a reckless gamble. It was a calculated one.

image.label: A director's chair facing a blank screen and a stack of 26 scripts
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 빈 촬영장에 감독 의자 하나, 앞에 아무것도 비치지 않은 스크린, 옆에 '26'이라고 적힌 대본 더미. 실제 회사 로고, 작품 로고, 배우 얼굴은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 2011. You're Netflix.
body: A well-known director, David Fincher, is shopping a drama based on a British series. Other networks are reportedly interested. Networks normally order a pilot, then decide.

options.text: Ask for a pilot first, like the networks do
options.feedback: You risk far less if it flops. But the producers may take a richer offer elsewhere, and you've learned nothing about making shows.

options.text: Commit to two full seasons upfront
options.feedback: You win the deal and signal you're serious. But you pay heavily before seeing a minute of footage.

options.text: Pass and keep licensing proven shows
options.feedback: Safer this year. But you stay dependent on studios that can raise prices or pull their shows.

choice.afterReveal: Netflix chose B. The next cards show why it was less reckless than it looks.

cards.title: The bet paid off.
body: Netflix ordered 26 episodes, reportedly for around $100 million. In February 2013, it released all 13 episodes of season one on the same day.

That year the show earned major Emmy nominations, a first for a streaming-only series, and Fincher won for directing the first episode. **House of Cards** told the world Netflix could make its own hits.

cards.title: Start with the base rate, then adjust it
body: The **base rate** is how often things like this usually work out. For new TV dramas, the base rate is poor. Most shows that get a pilot never become a lasting series.

Netflix had evidence a network didn't have. As *The New York Times* reported, its viewing data showed many subscribers had watched the original British series, Fincher's films, and films with the planned lead actor. Those audiences overlapped. The general odds became odds for *this* show and *these* viewers.

image.label: Three overlapping circles of viewers with a bright center
image.brief: 벤 다이어그램 인포그래픽. 세 원에 각각 "Watched the British original", "Watched the director's films", "Watched the lead actor's films" 라벨. 세 원이 겹치는 가운데 부분만 밝게 강조. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three questions behind the bet.
body: Netflix didn't need certainty. It needed better odds and a loss it could survive.

breakdown.label: Better than average
breakdown.detail: Viewing data pointed to a ready-made audience

breakdown.label: Bigger than one show
breakdown.detail: New subscribers, press, and proof it could make originals

breakdown.label: Painful, not fatal
breakdown.detail: A flop would hurt, but not end the company

cards.callout: Skipping the pilot cost more upfront, but it won the deal.

cards.title: Better odds are not a sure thing.
body: Data shifted the odds. It didn't guarantee a hit. Netflix has since paid for plenty of shows that were cancelled quickly, and we tend to remember the winners.
Some risks never show up in data. In 2017, Netflix cut ties with the show's lead actor after misconduct allegations. A good decision can still end badly, so judge the reasoning, not just the result.

cards.title: Same move, inside a company.
body: A team at a large manufacturer asks for budget to launch a new product line. A director says most new lines fail. That's the base rate, and it's a fair starting point.

The team's answer isn't "trust us." It's evidence: three existing customers have already placed trial orders. That moves the odds for this line, not lines in general. The director can then size the budget so a miss stings but doesn't sink the division.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: You run two busy noodle restaurants. Your chef wants to open a third place serving Korean fried chicken. You know many new restaurants struggle in their first years.

options.text: Don't open. The odds say it will probably fail
options.feedback: You avoid the risk, but you treat the general odds as yours without checking. Your customers and chef may change them.

options.text: Add the chicken as a weekend special for two months, track repeat orders, then decide
options.feedback: For the cost of some extra frying, you swap the general odds for evidence from your own customers before signing a lease.

options.text: Sign a long lease now. The chef has a great track record
options.feedback: A strong chef does improve the odds. But a new cuisine is a different bet, and a long lease makes the downside large.

cards.title: A bold bet can still be a careful one.
body: Start with how often things like this usually work. Adjust with evidence that's specific to you. Then bet an amount you can afford to lose.
**Try it today:** pick one risky idea on your list. Write down the usual odds, one piece of evidence that changes them for you, and the most you could lose.
